title: Nothing to hand over: MFA and passkeys

narration: Say this is Maya.
Each morning, she types her password,
and her work account opens.
beats.visual_intent: Maya at her desk in a light office; her laptop screen fills most of the frame: a plain sign-in page, the password dots type in, the page turns to 'Welcome, Maya'

grounding.claim: Maya and her sign-in are an invented example

narration: Say that password leaked from another site.
Someone else types it, far away.
It opens for them too.
beats.visual_intent: the frame splits: Maya's desk on the left, a second plain desk on the right with a person seen from behind; the same sign-in page on their screen, the same dots, the same 'Welcome, Maya'

grounding.claim: the leak and the stranger are an invented example
passwords leaked from other sites are reused to break in
the site cannot tell that person from Maya

narration: A password is something you know.
Anyone who knows it looks like Maya.
beats.visual_intent: both screens side by side showing the same welcome; an equals sign settles between them; the two people are different, the screens are identical

grounding.claim: a password is something you know; anyone who learns it looks like you

narration: So Maya adds a second step:
a code from her phone.
beats.visual_intent: Maya's screen moves past the password to 'Enter the code'; her phone on the desk lights with six digits; she types them and the welcome returns

grounding.claim: Maya's second step is an invented example
MFA adds a second factor such as a code from your phone

narration: The thief tries again.
The password works. Then, enter the code.
The code is on Maya's phone. They stop.
beats.visual_intent: split again: the thief's screen accepts the password, then stops on 'Enter the code' with an empty box and a blinking cursor; across the split, Maya's phone lights with a code she did not ask for and stays on her desk

grounding.claim: the second attempt is an invented example
without the second factor a thief with the password cannot sign in

narration: That is MFA, multi-factor authentication.
Two kinds of proof: something you know,
something you have, or something you are.
beats.visual_intent: close on Maya's desk: the password field, her phone, her fingertip on the phone; each lights and takes a short label as it is named

grounding.claim: MFA asks for two or more kinds of proof: know, have, are

narration: Microsoft researchers checked their own business accounts.
MFA cut the risk by a little over 99 percent.
Their data, not a guarantee.
beats.visual_intent: beside the thief's stopped screen, two plain bars: risk without MFA, full; risk with MFA, shrinking to a sliver; '99.22%' named last with who measured it in small type under it

grounding.claim: a Microsoft study found MFA cut the risk of compromise by 99.22 percent
it is the vendor's own data and a reduction, not a guarantee

narration: So the thief changes plan.
Maya gets a link to sign in.
The page looks exactly like hers.
Only the address is different.
beats.visual_intent: Maya's screen, large: a message with a link; the link opens a page identical to her sign-in; the address bar above it, large, reads a look-alike address beside the real one

grounding.claim: the link and the look-alike page are invented
a fake page copies a real login page

narration: She types her password, then her code.
Does the thief get in?
Decide before it plays.
beats.visual_intent: on the look-alike page Maya's password dots type in, then her code; the frame holds and the question drops in over the split, then silence

grounding.claim: the question sets up the relay shown next

recall.prompt: MFA is on. Maya types her password and her code into a page that only looks real. Does the thief get in?
recall.answer: Yes: the page passes both to the real site while the code is still valid.

beats.misconception: once MFA is on, a phishing page cannot get into my account

narration: Yes. The fake page passes on what she types,
into the real site, while the code still works.
The thief is in.
beats.visual_intent: split screen: as each character appears on Maya's look-alike page, the same character appears on the thief's real sign-in page a moment later; the code lands, the thief's screen says 'Welcome, Maya'

grounding.claim: the relay is shown on the invented example
the fake page collects the password and code and the attacker uses them at the real site while the code is valid

narration: The code felt like hers alone.
But anything you type, a fake page can ask for.
beats.visual_intent: Maya's phone and her typed code side by side; the typed code lifts off her screen and drifts across the split to the thief's side

grounding.claim: a typed code can be collected by a fake page

narration: Now give Maya a passkey.
It lives on her phone,
unlocked by fingerprint, face or PIN.
beats.visual_intent: her phone large in the frame; a key settles inside it behind the glass; her thumb touches the screen and it unlocks

grounding.claim: Maya's passkey is an invented example
a passkey is kept on the device and unlocked with a fingerprint, face or PIN

narration: The site asks a fresh question.
Her phone signs the answer,
stamped with the page's address.
The secret never leaves the phone.
beats.visual_intent: the real sign-in page sends a small question to the phone; the phone sends back an answer card stamped with the real address; the key stays inside the phone the whole time

grounding.claim: the device signs a fresh challenge and the private key stays on the device
the signed answer includes the address of the page that asked

narration: Same fake page.
This time there is nothing to type.
Her phone sees the wrong address, and stays silent.
The thief has nothing to pass on.
beats.visual_intent: the look-alike page with the address bar shown very large, the extra word marked; the phone checks it and stays silent; across the split, the thief's screen waits with nothing arriving

grounding.claim: the second phishing attempt is an invented example
a passkey made for one site cannot be used by a look-alike site
there is no code to type, so a fake page has nothing to pass on

narration: Google saw the same order on its own accounts.
Against targeted attacks, a texted code blocked 76 percent.
A phone prompt, 90.
Security keys alone: no one fell.
beats.visual_intent: three plain bars rise one per phrase, labelled texted code, phone prompt, security keys; the third bar carries the words no one fell instead of a number

grounding.claim: a texted code blocked 76 percent of targeted attacks
a phone prompt blocked 90 percent of targeted attacks
no user with only security keys fell to targeted phishing

narration: Their accounts, so read the direction.
Nothing here is unbreakable,
but any second factor beats none.
beats.visual_intent: the bars stay; one line settles under them; the third bar keeps a thin outline to say it is not a wall

grounding.claim: these are the platform's own accounts; read the pattern
phishing-resistant is not unbreakable
any MFA is better than none

narration: One last turn.
Maya's phone asks: is this you signing in?
It is not. Then again, and again.
beats.visual_intent: back at Maya's desk; her phone shows a sign-in prompt with Approve and Deny; a second and third prompt stack on top

grounding.claim: the repeated prompts are an invented example
attackers who have the password send prompt after prompt

narration: Someone has her password, and wants a tap.
She denies it, and shares no code.
beats.visual_intent: Maya's thumb on Deny; the prompts fall away; across the split, the thief's screen reads denied

grounding.claim: a prompt you did not start can mean someone has your password; refuse it and share no code

narration: A password can be copied.
A code can be passed on.
A passkey answers only the real site.
beats.visual_intent: the three things from the story side by side: the password field, the typed code, the phone with its key; each shows its outcome as it is named

grounding.claim: a password can be copied and used by anyone
a typed code can be relayed
a passkey answers only the site it was made for

narration: So, turn on a second factor.
Pick a passkey when offered.
Refuse any prompt you did not start.
on_screen: Refuse any prompt you did not start
beats.visual_intent: three short lines, each appearing as it is said

grounding.claim: any MFA beats none
passkeys resist phishing
refuse prompts you did not start

narration: With a passkey,
Maya has nothing to hand over.
beats.visual_intent: back to Maya at her desk, the opening sign-in, calm; the thief's desk across the split goes dark

grounding.claim: Maya is the invented example
with a passkey there is nothing to type or pass on
